note: The StoreCatalog mirror remains the cipher-selection authority for its six stores. durableStores is the broader in-place-upgrade compatibility register: every process-owned durable authority names its owner, recovery class, format, write behavior, reconciliation, implementation, and evidence. HARDENING_REQUIRED rows are an explicit tempdoc-617 ratchet; the gate forbids adding an unnamed gap. Tempdoc 879 added two required per-row answers. pathVerification: LITERAL means ONE implementationSources file contains the string literal of every segment of the declared path - a union across several files does not count, because that made LITERAL satisfiable by adding an unrelated file that merely mentions the missing word; COMPOSED means the path is assembled at runtime, and pathVerificationNote must say by what. encryption: SEALED_BY_STORE_CIPHER = the StoreCatalog cipher seals it; UNSEALED_KEY_ROOT = it IS the key root and cannot be sealed by the key it holds; UNSEALED_EXTERNAL_AUTHORITY = the bytes belong to the user or an operator, not the app; UNSEALED_NO_JVM_CIPHER = Shell-owned, written by Rust with no reach to the JVM StoreCipher; UNSEALED_DERIVED_OS_DISK_ENCRYPTION = StoreCatalog's Framing.OPAQUE position, a derived/rebuildable store that does hold user-derived content in the clear and is covered by OS disk encryption only; UNSEALED_GAP = no structural reason, simply not sealed yet; NOT_APPLICABLE = there is nothing here worth sealing. UNSEALED_GAP, UNSEALED_DERIVED_OS_DISK_ENCRYPTION and NOT_APPLICABLE are all claims about what the bytes hold, so the gate requires an encryptionNote on each saying what the file actually contains - before 879 NOT_APPLICABLE was the one value nobody had to justify, and it was standing in for both 'nothing sensitive' and 'the user's own document text'. Known limit of the LITERAL check: it matches string literals, so it cannot tell a path constant from a same-named error-message label - a few rows (agent-runs, memories, conversations) are LITERAL-green via a CorruptDurableStoreException store label rather than a path constant, which means a rename of those directories could pass. Closing that needs the gate to recognise resolve(...)-shaped occurrences specifically; tracked in tempdoc 879. nonDurableWriteSites is the OTHER answer the coverage check accepts: a production source the write-site scanner flags that holds no durable state at all, so there is no recovery, upgrade or encryption policy to state for it. The bar is that every path it writes is scratch - process-scoped, regenerated on demand, and outside the data dir - so losing or deleting the file costs a recomputation and nothing else. It is not an escape hatch for a durable store whose row is inconvenient to write: if deleting the file would lose user-visible state, it belongs in durableStores. TempFileManager is JVM/OS temp scratch; ExtractionSandboxFactory writes one JVM temp file for the extraction child's startup probe and deletes it in the same method (tempdoc 885 item 14). THIS REGISTER IS A WIRE CONTRACT, NOT DOCUMENTATION. Two consumers read durableStores at RUNTIME, and a row is a commitment to both. (1) modules/shell/src-tauri/src/updater.rs embeds it with include_str! (:31-32) and deserialises every row into LocalDurableStore, whose current_version is a u32 with NO serde default - so ONE row missing currentVersion makes the whole register unparseable and validate_store_compatibility rejects EVERY release descriptor. (2) modules/ui UpgradeReconciliationProbe.loadOwnerRegister (:196-225) builds the closed owner set for /api/upgrade/reconcile and returns an EMPTY register with a configuration error if ANY row has status != READY, which makes reconcile answer 409 and blocks in-place upgrades outright. Both were discovered the hard way in PR #604, which added six HARDENING_REQUIRED rows and broke both consumers at once. (3) A THIRD consumer, named in tempdoc 909: scripts/release/app-release-assets.mjs:77-80 GENERATES every release descriptor's compatibility table from durableStores and throws on any row that is not READY, so a non-READY row does not merely fail a gate - it makes the release assets unbuildable. Its test is scripts/release/app-release-assets.test.mjs. Consequences for an author: a row change is a wire change; HARDENING_REQUIRED is not a documentation tier but a refusal signal, and knownCompatibilityGaps is empty because the tempdoc-617 conversion finished - re-populating it turns upgrades off. Add a row only when it can be READY. DISCOVERY (wave-1 residue R1): the write-site scanner keys on write CALLS in code (scripts/governance/lib/persistence-write-scan.mjs strips comments, keeps literals), not on a "durable anchor" word appearing anywhere in the file text. The retired rule decided by reading English prose, which discovered ExtractionSandboxFactory via a javadoc sentence and missed ExtractionSandboxCommand's real argfile write. It over-discovers by design -- benchmarks, SSOT generators and the agent file tools all write to disk -- and each costs one honest nonDurableWriteSites line. nonDurableWriteSites entries are now { path, reason }: the classification is a claim, and every other row here justifies its claims. The broadened scan also found EIGHT files writing durable state no row owns. They were parked in pendingDurableClassification, not forced into durableStores: each needed a settled corruption policy and a recovery/preservation test before it could be READY, and a non-READY row would disable in-place upgrade outright (see the wire-contract paragraph above). Tempdoc 909 (wave-1 residue R4) did that work and drained the list to empty; the block and its cap of 8 remain as the ratchet for the next one. ROOTS (tempdoc 909): a fourth storage root, USER_INDEXED_ROOTS, joins DATA_DIR / AI_HOME / PROGRAM_DATA_OR_DATA_DIR. It exists for exactly one row - the user's own documents, which the agent's file-operations tool moves, copies and deletes in place. That authority is real and durable, but it lives under none of the app-owned roots, so before 909 it could not be written down at all: the register named the undo JOURNAL and not the thing the journal is about.

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSON holding the user's UI preferences, including the configured local model path and other machine-local settings. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: JSON envelope v1 around legacy UiSettings object
durableStores.corruptionNote: Unparseable file is moved to settings.json.corrupt-<timestamp>, defaults are loaded, and LifecycleReasonCode.SETTINGS_RESET_FROM_CORRUPT is raised as a WARN condition (ADR-0008, tempdoc 882 item 24). A future schemaVersion still fails loud (futureVersionRefusalTest). Test methods: readWrite_malformedStateIsQuarantinedAndDefaulted and readWrite_saveAfterRecoveryClearsRecoveryAndFiresCallback in the tests file below; the refusal is readWrite_futureVersionIsRefusedWithoutOverwrite.

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSONL of every governed action the user or agent took - operation ids, argument projections, and outcomes. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: append-only JSONL of ActionLedgerProjection wire rows, size-rotated (4 MB x 8 generations)

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSON recording which capability families the user durably granted the agent. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: JSON grant envelope v1

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: PluginAllowlistStore receives its file from the caller (PluginAllowlistStore.java:46) and holds no path literal at all. The whole path is composed at the wiring site as the settings file's sibling - LocalApiServer.java:189, b.settingsStore.settingsPath().resolveSibling("plugin-allowlist.json") - so the ui segment comes from UiSettingsStore.java:122 and only the base name is ever written literally.
durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSON of the SHA-256 hashes of plugin artifacts an operator explicitly trusted. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: JSON allowlist envelope v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: A single on/off capture preference. No user content, no path, nothing that discloses anything about the machine.
durableStores.format: JSON preference object v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: An inventory of the AI packs the app itself installed under AI Home - pack ids, versions, and the files each pack owns. Every value is app-distributed asset metadata; no user content, no user-chosen path.
durableStores.format: JSON envelope v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: The install bill of materials: model package ids, the variant/precision chosen per model, the detected hardware profile, and the app's own models directory (InstallContract.java:33-40). Machine and app-install facts only - no user content and no user-chosen path.
durableStores.format: JSON record v2
JSON KeystoreRecord v1
JSON policy envelope v1
encrypted JSON envelope v1 around legacy record arrays

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: Only the base name is a literal (RunEventStore.java:254, runDir(sessionId).resolve("events.ndjson")); RunEventStore receives its rootDir (RunEventStore.java:56) and the session directory is the run id. The agent-runs prefix is composed at the wiring site - HeadAssembly.java:429, dataDir.resolve("agent-runs") - and StoreCatalog.java, which was listed here, only declares that dirName; it writes nothing.
durableStores.format: append-only NDJSON event envelope v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSON transaction log of agent file mutations, including the absolute source and destination paths it moved or rewrote. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: JSON transaction log v2 (v2 adds executed[].destinationDigest for COPY)
durableStores.versionNote: v2 (tempdoc 909 items 7/8) added executed[].destinationDigest - the content identity a COPY-undo must match before it deletes the file. Purely additive: no field was removed or re-shaped, so v0 and v1 journals still read (FileOperationLogTest.legacyV1JournalRemainsReadable). A v1 entry's ABSENT digest is load-bearing rather than a gap: it is what tells the undo it cannot prove identity, so it preserves the file instead of deleting it. The bump exists so an OLDER app refuses a v2 journal loudly instead of undoing it under v1's weaker guarantee.

durableStores.format: encrypted append-only NDJSON record envelope v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext NDJSON of query/passage training triples mined from the user's own corpus - each row carries a synthetic_query generated from one of the user's documents plus that document's id (GplTrainingTripleStore.java:369-371). Derived and regenerable from the source documents, so it is deliberately unsealed and covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: append-only NDJSON with documented legacy and extended rows

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext JSON naming every filesystem root the user indexes - absolute paths that describe the user's disk layout. Nothing structural prevents sealing it; nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: JSON envelope v1 around legacy list or unversioned object; each root entry carries an optional `collection` label (tempdoc 885 §UD open item 4). Additive within v1 and forward-compatible in one direction only: an older build READS a newer file (it ignores the field), but persistRoots is a FULL_REWRITE, so if an older build then writes the file the labels are dropped and every root falls back to the default collection.

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: Only the base name is a literal (KnowledgeServer.java:480, dataDir.resolve("jobs.db")). SQLite itself creates the -wal and -shm sidecars, and the backup paths are composed from the database path (SqliteJobQueue.java:2010-2011; KnowledgeServer.java:2629-2630) - none of those sidecar or backup names exists as a standalone path literal.
durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext SQLite. Indexing-job rows are keyed on the user's absolute file paths, so the queue describes the user's disk layout in the clear - the same data class the watched-roots row calls an UNSEALED_GAP, but here it is StoreCatalog's stated Framing.OPAQUE position: a DERIVED queue rebuildable from the watched roots, covered by OS disk encryption only. The document_identity table adds only a SHA-256 path hash, a content-independent random uid, and timestamps; it stores no raw path or content-derived identity.
durableStores.corruptionNote: document_identity is restored indirectly: the existing pre-migration jobs.db backup can predate schema v11, so after backup restore (or a fresh queue rebuild when no backup exists) the Worker imports missing parent doc_id/doc_uid pairs from the serving Lucene index before indexing starts (KnowledgeServer.java:309-320, DocumentIdentityBootImport.java:50-110), streaming them in transactions of 1000. Existing identity rows remain authoritative during normal and mid-migration restarts. Since v12 the scan is a seeding step, not a per-boot pass: it runs only when document_identity is empty or document_identity_import has no row for the serving generation, because every later parent resolves its uid through the store. A live parent whose doc_id/doc_uid docvalues are missing or blank is counted in parents_skipped and re-mints at its next admission rather than failing the boot. Recovery limit: if the identity rows and their backup are lost and the serving Lucene index is also lost or unreadable, the old random uids cannot be reconstructed; later admission mints new uids, so uid-keyed derived or feedback links to the lost identities can become orphaned. That is a total-data-loss boundary, not a recoverable migration case.
durableStores.format: SQLite WAL schema v12

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: The index base path is resolved from configuration (ResolvedConfigBuilder.java:963, dataDir.resolve("index").resolve(collection)), so the index/<collection> prefix is not a literal in the owning component. Under it the layout IS literal - IndexGenerationManager.java:58-62 declares "indices", "state.json", "state.json.prev" - but the sibling recovery markers are composed as <generation dir name> + ".rebuild-pending" / ".clean-shutdown" (IndexRecoveryMarker.java:29,37; CleanShutdownMarker.java:28,36).
durableStores.encryptionNote: The largest plaintext user-content store in the product: the Lucene index stores the user's document text verbatim in stored fields (FieldMapper.java:370,380,382,393,395,410 use Field.Store.YES / StoredField), alongside the source paths. StoreCatalog frames it OPAQUE - a DERIVED store rebuildable from the source documents - so it is deliberately unsealed and covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: Lucene generations plus state v2 and generation manifest v1

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: MigrationProgressStore.java:33 resolves "migration_progress.json" against an injected indexBasePath; the index/<collection> prefix is configuration-resolved, not a literal in this component.
durableStores.encryptionNote: Mostly counters, but the snapshot also writes last_path - the absolute path of the last user file the enumerator walked (MigrationProgressStore.java:89) - so it holds one user document path in the clear. Derived from the in-flight migration and deleted-and-recomputed on any problem, so it is deliberately unsealed and covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: JSON status v1

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: Only the base name is a literal (DisambiguationService.java:50, dataDir.resolve("entity-clusters.db")). SQLite creates the -wal and -shm sidecars itself, so neither name exists as a literal.
durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext SQLite. entity_overrides records the user's own merge/split decisions and entity_clusters holds entity surface forms mined from the user's documents (EntityClusterSchema.java:8,15,41). Worker-owned, but the Worker is a JVM - unlike the Rust shell rows there is no reachability bar, only that nothing seals it today.
durableStores.format: SQLite WAL schema v1

durableStores.encryptionNote: Which inference runtime variant is active and whether it came up: variant name, health, an activation error code from a closed vocabulary, and timestamps (RuntimeActivationService.java:1434-1441). No user content.
durableStores.format: JSON runtime status, currently unversioned

durableStores.encryptionNote: Progress of an AI-pack import: which pack id is staging or installed and how far it got. App asset-management state only; no user content.
durableStores.format: JSON import status, currently unversioned

durableStores.encryptionNote: Who is running right now and where: instance id, process ids, loopback ports, the app's own data directory, and reachability/shutdown classification per instance (RuntimeManifestPublisher.java:40). Process bookkeeping only; no user content.
durableStores.format: atomic current manifest plus append-only instance history

durableStores.encryptionNote: Round-robin numeric time series, one datasource per curated low-cardinality metric (RrdMetricStore.java:45,183). Numbers against fixed metric names - no free text, no paths, no user content; the high-cardinality streams that can carry a document path go to telemetry/*.ndjson instead.
durableStores.format: RRD metric files derived from catalog

durableStores.encryptionNote: Model weights and runtime binaries the app downloaded or bundled - and only those, since the ownership rule limits this row to files a verified managed manifest names. Publicly distributed artifacts identical on every install; nothing user-derived to protect (files NOT claimed by a manifest are the byo-ai-assets row).
durableStores.ownershipRule: Only files named by a verified managed manifest are app-owned.
durableStores.format: manifest-owned downloaded or bundled model/runtime assets
durableStores.derivedCacheNote: Beyond the manifest-named assets, three APP-GENERATED caches live under models/** beside the file they derive from: <model>.optimized / .opt-meta / .cuda.* (OnnxSessionCache.java:29-32) and <model>.sha256 (Sha256SidecarCache.java:31,48). They are not manifest-named and are not user-supplied, so neither this row's ownershipRule nor byo-ai-assets described them. They are rebuildable at a cost (a 30s+ re-optimization, a 100-400ms rehash), never user data. Recorded here rather than split into a row of their own; splitting is the open option.

durableStores.ownershipRule: Files not named by a verified managed manifest remain user-owned.
durableStores.format: user-provided opaque model and runtime assets not named by a managed manifest
user-managed plugin manifest and JavaScript source

JSON anti-rollback sequence v1

durableStores.format: nonce-bound JSON shutdown receipt v1

The receipt CONTRACT is unchanged - same filename, same schemaVersion 1, same nonce and preparation binding - only its owner moved.

durableStores.encryptionNote: The id of the loaded model, plus a transition log of fromMode/toMode/reason/success/durationMs/generation (NdjsonInferenceTransitionLog.java:161-172). A closed vocabulary of lifecycle phases and reason codes - no prompt text, no completion text, no user content.
durableStores.format: runtime identity cache plus bounded transition telemetry

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext diagnostics that do carry user-derived content: the exported span attributes include doc.path and http.target (NdjsonSpanExporter.java:45,59), so indexed document paths and request query strings land in telemetry/*.ndjson, and crashes/*.json records the raw exception message plus stack trace (CrashReporter.java:101-102), which for an indexing failure names the file being read. Derived, bounded, and pruned rather than recovered, so it is deliberately unsealed and covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: bounded diagnostic NDJSON and JSON artifacts

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: The fatal-reason marker name IS a literal (WorkerFatalReasonMarker.java:29), but the two index markers are composed as <active generation dir name> + ".rebuild-pending" / ".clean-shutdown" against a configuration-resolved index path (IndexRecoveryMarker.java:29,37; CleanShutdownMarker.java:28,36).
durableStores.encryptionNote: Signal files, not data files: the two index markers carry meaning by existing, and worker-fatal-reason holds one reason code - its only production writer passes the INDEX_CORRUPT constant (KnowledgeServer.java:758-759; WorkerFatalReasonMarker.java:27). No message text, no path, no user content.
durableStores.format: single-use worker recovery and clean-shutdown marker files

durableStores.encryptionNote: Owner metadata for an OS file lock: the holding process's PID and its start timestamp, written so a later process can tell a live owner from a dead one (AppInstanceLock.java:121-122,157-172). PID and timestamp only; no user content.
durableStores.format: process ownership lock and PID marker files
durableStores.mmapNote: HISTORICAL. worker_signal.lock matched this row's *.lock glob exactly without being a PID marker: it was the memory-mapped Head<->Worker IPC region holding port, heartbeat and PID bytes, recreated each launch. Lane F stage A item A10 deleted both ends of it (MainSignalBus, MmfWorkerSignalBus) when the two processes became one JVM, so no such file is written any more. The note is kept because the *.lock glob is unchanged and a reader still has to know the row does not cover a mapped region.

durableStores.encryptionNote: Plaintext Markdown holding the agent's final answer to the user plus the title, path and excerpt of every document it grounded that answer in (AgentHistoryIndexer.java:141-164) - user-derived content in the clear. It is a DERIVED projection of the sealed agent-runs terminal event and is re-derivable from it, and it must stay readable as an ordinary file because the Worker process ingests it BY PATH over the explicit-collection ingest API (:124) - sealing it would break the only thing it exists for. Covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: one Markdown transcript per finished agent run, keyed by session id
durableStores.corruptionNote: A transcript that is missing, empty, or does not start with the header renderTranscript always writes is re-derived from the run's terminal done/error event and re-indexed (AgentHistoryIndexer.reconcileNow, run at boot and again on key unlock from HeadAssembly). When the run is NOT available - deleted, or the store locked on an encrypted install - the bytes on disk are left EXACTLY as they are and the transcript is simply not re-indexed. It is never deleted: a locked store is indistinguishable from an empty one at this layer (the trap AgentRunReconciler documents), so a drop-what-cannot-be-rebuilt rule would erase the user's whole agent history on the first locked boot. That is why this is not REGENERATE_OR_DROP_DERIVED_HISTORY, the nearest existing value.

durableStores.encryptionNote: Per-file download history for the AI install: the target path inside the app's own models directory, the registry URL it was fetched from, attempt and failed-pass counts, the last transport error string, a timestamp, and the transport tier that pass started at (InstallAttemptMemory.java:54-60). App-install and registry facts only - no user content and no user-chosen path.
durableStores.format: JSON record v1: {version, files: {targetPath -> Attempt}}
durableStores.corruptionNote: load() discards an unreadable, truncated or version-mismatched file and yields an EMPTY memory (InstallAttemptMemory.java:78-89), which reproduces the pre-824 behaviour exactly: transport tier 0, no terminal verdict, Repair still offered. The history rebuilds itself from subsequent install passes. Stated honestly: the version guard is an equality test, so a FUTURE version is discarded rather than preserved, and the next transport failure rewrites the file as v1 - the cost is one install's retry history, and losing the memory must never lose the install. Since tempdoc 909 the write goes through AtomicFileWrites, so a torn file is no longer reachable through the app's own writes.

durableStores.encryptionNote: Four aggregate numbers about the corpus at the last GPL evaluation: document count, triple count, an ISO timestamp, and a MIME-type histogram (GplEvalSnapshot.java:38-42). MIME TYPES and counts, never file names, paths or text - nothing here identifies a document.
durableStores.format: JSON snapshot of corpus state at the last GPL evaluation
durableStores.corruptionNote: An absent, empty or unparseable snapshot loads as null (GplEvalSnapshot.load), and GplRevalidationTrigger reads a null last-evaluation as 'first evaluation' - so the recovery IS the evaluation: it re-runs and save() rewrites the file. The cost is one extra evaluation; trusting half a snapshot would instead SKIP an evaluation the corpus needs. Reported at WARN once per file, not once per read, because load is published as a per-request Supplier (HeadAssembly.headInfraRegistry).

durableStores.encryptionNote: Aggregate GPL calibration statistics: per-bucket triple counts and contribution rates, a numeric parameter sweep, the selected configuration and a generated-at timestamp (GplStage3aAnalysisReport.java:31-46, GplStage3bBranchFusionReport.java:41-76). Counts, rates and sweep parameters only - no query text, no document id, no path.
durableStores.format: write-only JSON diagnostic reports written beside the triple store
durableStores.corruptionNote: Nothing in production reads either report back - the only production references are GplJobCoordinator's write(...) calls (:738, :747), which log the path and nothing else. So a torn or garbage report costs exactly one rerun of the analysis, which rewrites it in full from the triple store. That is a claim, not an assumption: GplStageReportWriteOnlyTest scans every production source tree for a reader and fails if one appears, and drives the torn-file rewrite. The write is deliberately NOT atomic (createDirectories + writeValue) because there is no reader to observe a partial file; if a reader is ever added, this row's recoverability and atomicity both change and the scan test is what forces that.

durableStores.encryptionNote: The child llama-server process's stdout AND stderr, redirected wholesale (LlamaServerOps.java:942-943). Its verbosity is llama-server's choice, not the app's: at higher verbosities the server prints request-shaped diagnostics, so prompt-derived text can land here, and the app reads the tail back for startup diagnostics. Named honestly rather than filed as NOT_APPLICABLE - it is a derived, bounded, rotated diagnostic that can hold user-derived text in the clear, covered by OS disk encryption only.
durableStores.format: plain-text process log, rotated on each launch, 3 generations retained
durableStores.corruptionNote: Nothing recovers this file: each launch rotates it to .1 (and .1 to .2, deleting .2) and starts a fresh one, so an unreadable, truncated or interleaved log is aged out by the next start rather than repaired. Before tempdoc 909 it had NO retention at all - appendTo across every launch for the life of the install. Retention is a constant (RETAINED_LOG_GENERATIONS = 3), not a config key, and matched WorkerSpawner's worker.log policy, which is where the app's one retention story for supervised-process logs came from; lane F stage A item A11 deleted that spawner and item A16 folded the Head's own log into <dataDir>/logs/engine.log (rolled by Logback's SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy, a different policy entirely), so llama-server.log is now the only log THIS policy governs (RETAINED_LOG_GENERATIONS = 3 is unchanged). No worker.log is written any more, and it never had a row here. Ordering is load-bearing: the live file is renamed aside FIRST and nothing is pruned until that succeeds, because on Windows the rename fails while a handle is open (a llama-server past the 5s kill timeout, an orphan, a handle not yet released) - pruning first would delete the oldest generation and shift the rest before discovering it cannot move the live file, leaving FEWER retained logs and a still-growing live file in exactly the crash-restart loop where retention matters. A .rotating file left by a failure between the two renames is bounded (the next launch replaces it) and is covered by the ownedPaths glob.

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: There is no path literal to check: the roots are whatever the user configured, read live from the indexing service through FileOperationExecutor's indexedRootsSupplier (:29, :50, :121-134), and the file names come from the agent's tool call. Every path is composed at runtime from those two, and the sandbox check - not a declared path - is what bounds them.
durableStores.encryptionNote: The user's own documents, in the user's own folders. The app moves, copies and deletes them on request; it does not own their bytes and must never re-encode or seal them.
durableStores.ownershipRule: The app owns NONE of these bytes. It may only mutate a path inside a currently-configured indexed root, on an approved WRITE-safety tool call, and it may DELETE one only to undo a COPY it can prove it made (see corruptionPolicy).
durableStores.format: the user's own files, mutated in place by the agent's file-operations tool
durableStores.corruptionNote: Undoing a COPY is a DELETE of what is, by then, an ordinary user file. It proceeds ONLY when the destination still holds exactly the content the journal recorded at copy time (SHA-256 for a file, a sorted path+size+hash digest for a tree; FileContentDigest). Three refusals, all preserving and all reported to the user by name: content no longer matches, the journal predates the recorded identity (schema v1, so identity cannot be proven), or the path has fallen outside the current indexed roots (tempdoc 875 C.6). The mtime conflict check (tempdoc 577 2.14 Root III) still runs first and still skips a since-edited target; it is kept because it catches an edit the digest cannot attribute, but it is no longer the last line of defence - a timestamp-preserving write made it silent. MOVE/RENAME undo relocates rather than deletes and needs no digest; MKDIR undo removes only an empty directory. TWO limits are stated rather than implied. (1) COST AND CAP: the digest is a full extra read of what was just copied, computed synchronously on the tool-call thread and again at undo - milliseconds for ordinary documents, seconds for a multi-gigabyte file or tree. Above FileContentDigest.MAX_DIGEST_BYTES (2 GiB) no digest is computed at all, so such a copy takes the same conservative branch a pre-v2 journal takes: preserved, not deleted, and reported as unverifiable. Refusing to delete an unverified multi-gigabyte file is the safe direction. (2) CHECK-THEN-DELETE WINDOW: the verify and the delete are not atomic, so a write landing in the microseconds between them is deleted unverified. Closing it would require an exclusive lock on a file the USER owns, held across both - which takes the user's document hostage to an undo and can itself fail on a file an editor has open. The window is a narrowing of an unbounded exposure (every timestamp-preserving edit, forever) to a microsecond one on an operation the user explicitly asked for; it is not a guarantee, and it is written down here so no reader mistakes it for one.

durableStores.encryptionNote: A single version token ("v2") recording which generation of the app's own bundled help documents has been ingested. App-distributed content only: no user document content, no user-chosen path, no credential.
durableStores.format: A bare version token, unversioned by construction
durableStores.note: Added at lane F item A19, and the reason it did not exist before is worth recording rather than quietly fixing: this write site was only ever COVERED by accident. KnowledgeServerBootstrap.java appeared in the retired worker-config-snapshot row's implementationSources (it was one of the files that handled the snapshot), so the coverage check saw the file as classified and never asked what ELSE it wrote. Removing that row exposed a genuine, unrelated durable artifact at KnowledgeServerBootstrap.java:867,901. The gate was right both times; the register was carrying a false negative. Deliberately NON_ATOMIC and untested: it is a one-token marker whose worst failure is re-ingesting a handful of bundled help files, so hardening it would cost more than the outcome it prevents — but that is now a stated judgement rather than an unexamined gap.

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: ShutdownRequest.pathIn resolves the literal "shutdown-request.v1.json" against an injected <dataDir>/runtime directory; the dataDir prefix is configuration-resolved, not a literal in this component.
durableStores.encryptionNote: Four fields, none of them user content: a reason enum, an epoch-millis deadline, an optional updater nonce and an issuer label. The nonce is a per-upgrade correlation token the updater already holds on both sides, not a secret, and the file exists only for the seconds between a supervisor deciding to stop the Engine and the Engine consuming it.
durableStores.format: JSON request v1
durableStores.reconciliation: There is nothing to reconcile: the file is a request, not a record. The Engine deletes it on consumption and the supervisor rewrites it if it still wants the Engine to stop. A malformed or unknown-reason file is logged and IGNORED rather than guessed at, because guessing a reason from a file caught mid-write could stop the product; the supervisor’s own deadline-then-kill covers the case where ignoring it was wrong.

durableStores.pathVerificationNote: The supervisor resolves the literal "supervisor.v1.json" against a <dataDir>/runtime directory it composes from the resolved data dir (scripts/dev/dev-runner.cjs supervisorStatePath). The dataDir prefix is configuration-resolved, not a literal, and the writer is JavaScript, so the register's literal check — which reads double-quoted strings only — could not speak about it either way.
durableStores.encryptionNote: There is no JVM anywhere near this file by design: the Engine's supervisor is deliberately not a JVM (design 7.1's `never` clause), so the store cipher is not available to either writer. The content is a state name, a restart count, an exit code with its reason label and the run's own ids — no user content and no secret.
durableStores.format: JSON supervisor state v1, plus an append-only JSONL mirror of the terminal record
durableStores.reconciliation: The live file is a claim about a process that may no longer exist, so it is never trusted across a supervisor's own lifetime: a supervisor rewrites it from `starting` on its first transition and every reader treats an absent file as UNSUPERVISED rather than as an error (stage B checklist Q7 (a) — the bare app-launcher shape of design 3.1 has no supervisor and must still boot). A corrupt file is deleted and rewritten by the next transition; nothing is recovered from it, because everything in it is re-derivable from the run that is happening now. The JSONL mirror is the exception and the reason it exists: the terminal `exhausted` record has to survive the moment the Engine and its supervisor are both gone, because the reader that needs it — the updater's dead-Engine path — arrives afterwards.
durableStores.note: Added at lane F stage B item B8 with one writer and completed at item B10 with the second. design 7.1 declares TWO implementations of one supervisor contract, and this row is where that stops being a claim about behaviour and becomes a claim about bytes: the dev-runner and the Tauri shell write the same field set into the same path, and the harness asserts the shared shape (kind, schemaVersion, state, incarnation, restartCount) from both adapters. Note also what this row does NOT do: it is EPHEMERAL/RESET, which is honest for live state, and the checklist's Q5 weighed moving it outside runtime/ to escape that classification and chose the mirror instead — an upgrade legitimately resets the live state, and the one record that must not be reset is the terminal one. The JSONL mirror is written by the dev-runner only at this stage; the shell's terminal record is the live file plus the updater's own reading of it (item B13), which is the case Q5 was actually about.

nonDurableWriteSites.reason: A conformance driver, not a product path: it writes the supervisor state file and the shutdown request into a THROWAWAY data directory the harness creates per case and deletes after (scripts/supervisor-conformance/adapters/tauri.mjs). The artifacts it produces are the ones `engine-supervisor-state` and `engine-shutdown-request` already classify; what this binary owns is the temp directory around them, and nothing in it survives the case that made it. It is discovered by the write-site scan because the scan reads modules/**/*.rs by construction — which is right, and the honest answer is this row rather than an exclusion.

Dev-only signal file, not a store: it deletes <dataDir>/runtime/dev-reload.request to consume a hot-reload poke written by an external dev tool. Nothing is ever written here (existence IS the signal) and nothing survives a restart, so there is no format, no version and nothing to recover. This is what is left of the memory-mapped signal bus lane F stage A item A10 deleted — the one signal that genuinely crossed a process boundary, re-homed from a byte onto a file.

pendingDurableClassification.note: Durable write sites the write-call scanner found that have NO durableStores row yet. This is NOT nonDurableWriteSites: every one of these holds state that survives, so classifying them as scratch would be the escape hatch this register forbids. It is also not a durableStores row, because a row is a runtime commitment on the upgrade path (again: see the note), and each of these needs a settled corruption policy plus a recovery/preservation test before it can be READY. `cap` is a ratchet: the list may not grow past it without a deliberate edit, so a later agent cannot quietly park a new store here. Every entry names its blocker. DRAINED to empty by tempdoc 909 (wave-1 residue R4): all eight became READY rows above, each after the product work its blocker named - a boot+unlock re-derivation for agent-history transcripts, an atomic write for install-attempts.json, a stated-and-tested absent-on-unparseable policy for the GPL eval snapshot, a source-scan test proving the two GPL stage-3 reports have no reader, bounded rotation for llama-server.log, and content-verified COPY-undo for the user's own documents. The block and its cap stay so the ratchet survives an empty list: a future write site may be parked here again, but only deliberately and only up to eight.
